title: The Kitchen of the Realm: Even the Commoners Ate Well in Ancient Osaka - Nautilus
gist: An Anthropological Science study reconstructs the diet of Edo-period Osaka commoners by analyzing their teeth and dental plaque, revealing what ordinary people ate in a booming domestic-trade hub during Japan's isolationist era.

insights.claim: During Japan's isolationist Edo period (1603-1868), international trade slowed to a trickle but domestic trade boomed, making Osaka a flourishing commercial and cultural hub with a vibrant commoner class.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Context on how internal commerce sustained a prosperous merchant class despite closed borders.
insights.locator: international trade slowed to a trickle

insights.claim: A study in Anthropological Science reveals what Edo-period Osaka commoners ate by analyzing their teeth, particularly dental plaque.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Shows dental plaque analysis can reconstruct historical diets of ordinary people, not just elites.
insights.locator: revealing what these commoners ate by looking at their teeth

insights.claim: Tooth wear patterns reveal the bulk of an ancient diet while isotopic analysis distinguishes broad food categories like corn versus rice and how much meat was consumed.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Explains the layered archaeological toolkit for inferring diet from human remains.
insights.locator: Distinct wear patterns, for example, offer a window into what composed the bulk of the diet.
